prize_parts.citation: For the proposal and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms made accuracy at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I opened with the quantum spin Hall effect (B012) and I now move to optical lattice clocks (B019). The chair asks what is discovered beyond better numbers. My answer, after reading Kroll, Johansson and Danielsson, is that the magic-wavelength condition is a discrete physical idea: it removes the lattice light shift to first order, so that thousands of atoms can be held without their motion limiting the measurement. That is a change in what can be measured, and it is reflected in the physics seen in the data (many-body and collisional effects in the systematic budget, gravitational redshift resolved over about a millimetre). I weigh reproducibility and stability of interpretation above everything else, and here the evidence is the strongest on the shortlist: independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB and NIST agree within agreed uncertainty budgets, and nobody doubts the result. The credit is also the cleanest available, a proposal-plus-realisation pair with Katori and Ye named by every supporter. B012 has the same kind of maturity but its credit problem (Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Zhang's death, the 3D pioneers) cannot be repaired within three names, and I do not want to prize a topic whose attribution we already know to be a compromise. I defer to Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson on atomic physics, and the fact that they, who know the field, converge on the same two names and the same physical argument counts for me as evidence, though I do not count heads as a substitute for the argument itself.
statement.case_against: The overlap with earlier metrology prizes (frequency comb 2005, ion control 2012, laser cooling 1997 and 2018) is real, and I raised it myself in round 1. A fair reading is that lattice clocks are a threshold crossing in precision spectroscopy and not a new state of matter or a new quantum phenomenon, which is the kind of discovery I am most drawn to. The priority record for the first strontium lattice clock (Katori, JILA, SYRTE) and the contributions of Lemonde and of Derevianko on the theory of magic wavelengths and shifts have not been checked by this committee, and I cannot judge them from my own field. The redefinition of the second is prospective and must not carry the case. Finally, I am moving partly because B012 has a credit gap I cannot close, which is a weaker reason than a positive physical preference, and I want that to be visible.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the optical lattice clock is a new measurement capability and not a refinement: Katori's magic-wavelength idea plus Ye's realisation to 10^-18 form a clean proposal-plus-realisation pair, with agreed uncertainty budgets across five laboratories.
responses.response: That is the argument that moved me. In round 1 I asked whether this was a discovery or a threshold, and your answer, that the magic-wavelength trap changes which systematic effects exist at all and thereby opens a regime, is more convincing than a statement about the accuracy figure. I would ask you to keep the citation on the trap and the instrument, as you propose, and not on the pending redefinition. I also take your own case_against seriously: the comb and ion-control prizes covered part of the toolbox, so the citation should say what is new, namely many-atom interrogation without motional shifts. If a check of the priority record for the first Sr lattice clock shows a different pair, I would reconsider the names.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B012 second but doubts it is ready as a prize configuration, since Zhang has died, the HgTe proposal is outside the credited names, and the 2016 prize covered topological phases; Johansson has also moved circuit QED to an alternative and B019 to first place.
responses.response: You are right on the credit, and after the chair's question on citation scope I think the narrow quantum spin Hall wording does not fully solve it: a citation to the 2D effect names Molenkamp as the experimentalist for a proposal that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made, and we cannot honestly fix that with three names. I still hold that the 2016 prize left the Z2 class untouched, so I keep B012 as my first alternative. On circuit QED, we agree to hold it, and I appreciate that you flagged your own WACQT interest as a reason to discount your view on B004. Where I remain unsure is your point that many-body effects are now visible in the clock systematics; I would like to see a reference to a published quantitative result before treating that as a distinct physics result and not an accuracy statement.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B047) with Bistritzer kept as third name, argues that the prize does not need a settled pairing mechanism, and disagreed with my earlier proposal to drop Bistritzer.
responses.response: I concede the Bistritzer point. The magic-angle result is the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper, and since the union MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero fits in three names there is no space argument for omission; I withdraw my earlier two-name suggestion. I also accept that a mechanism is not strictly needed for the existence of the phases. My remaining hesitation is a matter of timing and of credit on the experimental side, since Cao, Fatemi and the 2018 first authors are not named and twist-angle disorder still limits reproducibility between samples. I will keep B047 as an alternative, not a preference, and I would treat it as a leading candidate in two or three years if the independent confirmation of the superconducting state continues. I do not think waiting is free, as you say, but I think a prize on a mature, firmly confirmed result loses less than a prize on one still being interpreted.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B047 as a theory-then-experiment discovery with a clean dated record (prediction 2011, discovery 2018), and holds a serious qualification about B012: three names cannot represent Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang or the 3D work, and Zhang has died.
responses.response: I agree with your qualification about B012, and it is the main reason I have moved off my first choice; I would add that I do not think the credit problem there is harder than for B047 only because of Zhang's death, but because the Kane-Mele proposal and the Molenkamp experiment were not the same line of work as the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that Molenkamp actually tested. On your own preference, I find the 'a number predicted, then found' structure compelling and it is why B047 stays my second alternative. We still differ on timing: I would give weight to eight years being short for a platform where the superconducting mechanism and sample-to-sample disorder are open, and to the fact that the experimental credit rests on a group leader. If the committee asks outside experts, I would suggest asking them the pairing-mechanism question for B047, since that would tell us whether waiting changes anything.

responses.point: Lindroth, an atomic theorist, ranks lattice clocks first and, in round 1, was asked by me whether 1e-18 is a physical discovery or a technical achievement; she also declared that she may overvalue B019 as an atomic theorist.
responses.response: I appreciate your declaration of a possible bias, and I treat your view as informed and not as a vote to be counted. As a non-specialist, I ask the narrower question: does the lattice-clock record show a physics result other than the accuracy figure? From the committee's exchange I accept that the magic-wavelength construction, together with resolved many-body and density shifts and the millimetre-scale redshift, is more than a number, and that is enough for me. I would keep theory out of the credited names, as you and Kroll do, but ask that the citation say clearly that the discovery is the trap and its physics, not the redefinition of the second.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record for the first Sr lattice clock and the status of Lemonde and Derevianko change the credited pair; I cannot judge this from condensed-matter physics.
Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice clock is a discovery of a new regime and not a precision milestone in a line already prized in 1997, 2005, 2012 and 2018.
Whether a narrow quantum spin Hall citation could ever be repaired for B012 without the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, in which case it should wait or be dropped.
How B047 will look in two or three years when the superconducting mechanism and sample disorder have had more study.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent. I work on electronic-structure theory and magnetism at Uppsala, have no stated personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and I defer to colleagues on atomic physics. I was Chair for the 2025 prize, which had no bearing on any shortlisted name.
